lines.text: fantasies born of our desires and dreams, or whether our
waiting for the future is so radical that we renounce all
such dreams and yet are cheerful in our confident waiting.
Do we step forward with confident trust into a future which
is shrouded in darkness for us, because our hope is set on
God's future, which surpasses all that we can desire or
conceive?
To be a Christian means to be one who waits for God's
future. Hence for the Christian perhaps all seasons are
essentially an Advent season. For Advent is characterized
above all by this note of expectation. Yes, so it is, and yet
it seems good to distinguish the season of Advent in the
round of the Church's year as the special time of expectation.
It is intended to remind us sharply of what we so easily and
so often forget, namely that, as Christians, we are expectant.
But also it should make us more certain of the fulfilment of
the promise, for it leads us on to that feast which is the very
symbol of fulfilment, the Feast of the Holy Nativity. Is it
merely a symbol of fulfilment? Or is it also already fulfilment
itself, in so far as fulfilment is possible in the context of our
earthly pilgrimage?
Yes, it is certainly fulfilment provided we celebrate the
feast in its true sense, by opening our hearts to the message of
the divine love which is rooted in the birth of Jesus Christ.
It depends on us, whether Christmas will signify for us a
real fulfilment. The more difficult it may seem to us this year
to keep Christmas with the joy normally associated with it,
so much the more should we remind ourselves that the true
Christian joy is promised to those who wait upon God. And
so all the heaviness which lies on our hearts may serve to
make us realize that we are the expectant ones who trust in
God. Thus we shall be prepared to receive the true Christ-
mas joy which will transform our human expectancy into a
trustful, glad and consoled waiting for the gift of God's
future.
